extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and scientifically literate readers interested in number theory and mathematical proof verification
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and community norms for judging the correctness, exposition, and publication-worthiness of a major mathematical proof (illustrated by the Mochizuki abc case). Focuses on verifiability, clarity, key-step justification, and publication ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent verifiability by non-insiders
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed proof should be understood and checked by independent experts beyond the author's immediate circle; broad independent confidence is required before the community accepts a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that only mathematicians in 'Mochizuki's orbit' vouched for the proof and that lack of other experts willing to say they are confident undermines acceptance. Verifiability includes the ability of multiple independent readers to follow and validate arguments off the record or publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and comprehensibility of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should avoid an impenetrable style — definitions, theorems, and proofs must be presented so that experts outside the author's immediate circle can follow the ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes long definitions followed by very short proofs and 'vast fields of trivialities followed by an enormous cliff of unjustified conclusions.' Good exposition means making the key ideas accessible and avoid producing a 'cloud of fog' for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full justification of critical steps and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Every critical step — especially centrally consequential corollaries — must be justified transparently; a single unresolved critical step can invalidate an entire claimed proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 3.12 is presented as central: 'Without it, there is no proof at all.' The community expects that such pivotal results have fully explained logic rather than terse or opaque arguments. If readers 'can't follow the logic after Figure 3.8', the proof is not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unjustified identifications between distinct objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must not make arbitrary identifications or conflate mathematical objects that should be regarded as distinct; such conflations can create false conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mochizuki accuses Scholze and Stix of misunderstanding by making arbitrary identifications, while Scholze and Stix claim the argument relies on identifications that render volume comparisons invalid. The criterion is to keep distinctions explicit and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring global consistency from local constructions (control of compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructions or measurements are defined locally (in different 'copies' or contexts), proofs must demonstrate how local data glue together globally without introducing uncontrolled distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dispute centers on volume measurements in several 'copies' of the real numbers arranged in a circle; local compatibility that fails to be globally consistent can change which inequality is being proved. Authors must control such compatibility factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible handling of dependencies on prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof relies on a large body of prior results (e.g., hundreds of pages), the dependence should be documented and made accessible enough that independent experts can trace and verify the logical chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mochizuki's papers refer back to roughly 500 pages of previous work, creating 'a sense of infinite regress.' Authors should avoid burying crucial arguments in an inaccessibly large corpus or should provide clear roadmaps and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of those who understand to teach and explain to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts who claim to understand the work must be able to explain its key ideas and make them comprehensible to other specialists; understanding should be communicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matthew Emerton is quoted: 'No expert who claims to understand the arguments has succeeded in explaining them to any of the (very many) experts who remain mystified.' Good proofs lend themselves to exposition in seminars, meetings, and written explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and precision in stating objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms of a proof should pinpoint precise places (lines, figures, lemmas) and articulate why the reasoning fails; vague sociological complaints are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholze and Stix identified a particular place ('after Figure 3.8 in the proof of Corollary 3.12') and distilled their objection to its essence; the article praises this pinpointing as useful to community assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to critique: provide coherent rebuttals and substantial revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An author must address identified gaps with thorough, coherent explanations and, if necessary, substantial revisions before the community should accept the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholze said 'this should not be considered a proof until Mochizuki does some very substantial revisions and explains this key step much better.' Mochizuki posted rebuttals, but the community expects clear, convincing fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and propriety in publication and editorial processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and authors must avoid conflicts of interest (e.g., an author being editor-in-chief of a journal publishing their own work) and ensure transparent peer review to preserve trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes controversy when Mochizuki was editor-in-chief of the journal in question and that 'editors generally recuse themselves in such situations.' Poor optics or lack of recusal undermines confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community vetting and consensus as part of proof acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond formal publication, mathematical proofs gain acceptance through broad community scrutiny and consensus; if only a small circle endorses a result, skepticism remains appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that between 12 and 18 mathematicians believed the proof was correct, but this limited backing contrasts with the wider community's inability to follow the work. Reputation helps attention but not substitute for broad vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of pedagogy and meetings to resolving disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops, dedicated meetings, and direct discussions between critics and authors are valuable mechanisms to clarify and resolve deep technical disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative describes a weeklong visit and dedicated meetings (e.g., 2015 Oxford meeting) as instrumental in distilling objections and attempts to communicate the proof's ideas; such interactions can accelerate resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate author reputation with correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: High stature of an author does not by itself guarantee correctness of a proof; arguments must stand or fall on their own merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece repeatedly notes Mochizuki's brilliance and Scholze/Stix's stature, but emphasizes that 'stature guarantees that mathematicians will pay attention' rather than proving correctness; community verification remains necessary.
